slides.text: When the non-cooperation movement started in India, under its influence, farmers in the Dhamtari region of Chhattisgarh protested against the tax imposed on the canal water of the British. This became known as the Kandel Canal Satyagraha.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Kandel village — flooded paddy fields, canal water flowing freely in August monsoon, a British tax notice nailed to a tree. Farmers standing firm, arms at their sides. Ink-wash illustration, deep greens and grey sky. Defiance without weapons.

slides.text: Dhamtari district. Kandel village. Seventy kilometres from Raipur. August 1920. The monsoon rains are heavy. The paddy fields are flooded. The farmers of Kandel are doing what they have always done — farming their land with their water.
slides.visualDescription: Aerial view of Kandel village in August monsoon — green paddy fields, flooded, the canal running alongside. Farmers working in the rain. A peaceful, industrious village at harvest time. The beauty of what is about to be threatened.

slides.text: The government's irrigation department accused the farmers of Kandel of stealing water from the canal. It was the month of August, it was raining heavily. There was enough water in the fields. Therefore, the charge of farmers stealing water from the canal was false.
slides.visualDescription: A British irrigation officer in colonial uniform, reading out the charge of water theft to assembled farmers. The canal flowing full beside him. The monsoon rain falling. The farmers looking at the sky, then at the canal, then at the officer. Absurdity as injustice.

slides.text: But the British irrigation department proceeded with the false charge. The policy of repression began: cattle seized during the farming season, Rs 4,030 confiscated from farmers. The punishment was real even when the crime was invented.
slides.visualDescription: British officers leading away farmers' cattle during the peak farming season. The farmers watching in distress — without their cattle, the harvest is impossible. Money confiscated. A family's year's work threatened by a false charge. Quiet devastation.

slides.text: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava stepped forward. Not a philosopher, not a national leader — a man from the community who simply refused to accept the false charge and the unjust punishment. He began organising the Kandel Canal Satyagraha.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — a man of the community, not a famous figure — standing in the flooded field, addressing the farmers of Kandel. His posture: firm, clear, unafraid. The farmers gathering around him. Leadership born from refusal.

slides.text: Pandit Sundarlal Sharma and Narayan Rao Meghawale joined the Satyagraha, widening its scope from a local dispute to a movement with Congress backing. What began as one village's refusal became a regional act of conscience.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma and Narayan Rao Meghawale arriving in Kandel — being received by Srivastava and the farmers. The handshake that connected the local movement to the national one. The Satyagraha growing in stature and scope.

slides.text: The Kandel Satyagraha became a model of disciplined non-violence. No weapons, no violence, no threats — only firm, organised refusal to accept an unjust tax. The farmers held their ground as surely as the earth holds the seed.
slides.visualDescription: The farmers of Kandel in a line facing the British officers — peaceful, disciplined, not moving. No weapons. No aggression. Just presence and refusal. The power of organised non-violence. The British not knowing what to do with men who simply stand.

slides.text: Meanwhile, December 1920. The Congress session was to be held in Nagpur. Sensing the opportunity, Pt. Sundarlal Sharma made a decision: Gandhi was travelling from Calcutta to Nagpur. He would intercept the journey and bring Gandhi to Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma with a railway timetable and a map. Tracing the route: Calcutta to Nagpur. Kandel to Raipur. A plan forming. The strategic mind of the freedom movement working. One journey intersecting another to change history.

slides.text: Sharma went to Calcutta because Gandhi was about to come from Calcutta to Nagpur. He found Gandhi and informed him about the Kandel Satyagraha. Gandhi agreed to stop at Raipur. A small detour that would echo for a century.
slides.visualDescription: Calcutta station — busy, crowded, December 1920. Sharma spotting Gandhi among the passengers. The meeting. Sharma speaking urgently, hands gesturing toward Chhattisgarh on an imaginary map. Gandhi listening, then nodding. Agreement. The detour decided.

slides.text: The parallel with Champaran was not lost on anyone. In 1917, Rajkumar Shukla had brought Gandhi from Calcutta to Champaran — the indigo farmers' Satyagraha. The British, hearing Gandhi was coming, formed a committee and conceded. The pattern was established.
slides.visualDescription: Champaran, 1917 on the left panel: Rajkumar Shukla leading Gandhi through indigo fields. Kandel, 1920 on the right: Pt. Sharma bringing Gandhi toward Chhattisgarh. The same pattern repeated. Gandhi as the weapon of the wronged. The Champaran template.

slides.text: When the British came to know that Gandhi was coming to support the farmers of Kandel, they immediately formed a committee to resolve it. The Champaran peasant movement had become successful in the same way. Now Kandel would follow.
slides.visualDescription: A British telegraph office receiving the urgent message: Gandhi is coming to Kandel. Officers in panic. A committee being hastily convened. Documents drafted for withdrawal of the order. The entire machinery of empire reacting to one man's travel itinerary.

slides.text: The British accepted the demands of Kandel Satyagrahis even before Mahatma Gandhi reached Raipur. The anti-farmer order was withdrawn. The confiscated cattle were returned. The Rs 4,030 was to be repaid. The Satyagraha had succeeded.
slides.visualDescription: The withdrawal order being signed. Cattle being returned to their owners. Farmers receiving back what was taken. Srivastava reading the concession document. Victory without a single blow struck. The power of organised truth against organised power.

slides.text: But Gandhi was still coming. The Satyagraha had won before his arrival, but the man who had made it win by the mere announcement of his journey — that man had not yet seen the land he changed. Chhattisgarh waited for him.
slides.visualDescription: The farmers of Kandel celebrating their victory — but looking down the road, toward Raipur, toward the direction Gandhi will come from. Their Satyagraha won, but they want to see the man whose name made it possible. The anticipation. The gratitude.

slides.text: Raipur in December 1920. Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla, Thakur Pyarelal Singh, Sakharam Dubey, and others are preparing. The platform is being decorated. Volunteers are being organised. The district is holding its breath.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station being decorated for Gandhi's arrival — flower garlands, volunteers in position, leaders in the front. Ravi Shankar Shukla directing the preparations. The whole district converging on the railway station. A city preparing for a moment.

slides.text: Gandhi was accompanied by the Ali brothers — Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali, leaders of the Khilafat Movement. Their presence underlined the unity of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements that Gandhi had woven into a single strand.
slides.visualDescription: Inside the train: Gandhi, Shaukat Ali, and Muhammad Ali in conversation. Three leaders, three faiths represented between them. The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements traveling together on the Calcutta-Nagpur line. Unity in transit.

slides.text: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — the man who started it all — sat with his farmers in Kandel, knowing the Satyagraha had succeeded. He had no way of knowing that what he started would eventually connect his village to a man who would shake an empire.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava in Kandel — sitting with farmers under a tree, the canal flowing peacefully beside them. The victory quiet and complete. He doesn't yet know that in a few days, Gandhi will stand in Dhamtari and speak his name to thousands.

slides.text: The Kandel Canal Satyagraha was a microcosm of everything the Non-Cooperation Movement stood for: the refusal of an unjust law, organised community resistance, moral rather than physical force, and the power of a collective will over an individual order.
slides.visualDescription: The elements of the Satyagraha laid out visually: farmers standing firm, the false charge document, the canal water, the cattle returned. A template. A proof of concept. What Gandhi had theorised, these farmers had practised in a monsoon-soaked village.

slides.text: On December 21, Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali addressed the Muslim gathering at Yateemkhana in Dhamtari. The Khilafat message and the Non-Cooperation message arriving together in a town where the Satyagraha had just succeeded.
slides.visualDescription: Yateemkhana, Dhamtari, December 21. A large Muslim gathering. Shaukat Ali at the podium — broad, commanding. Muhammad Ali beside him. The Khilafat Movement speaking in the heartland of the Kandel Satyagraha. Two movements converging in one town.

slides.text: Abbas Bhai drove Gandhi from Raipur to Dhamtari in his motor — the only motor available. When a police officer tried to stop the bus driver from taking Gandhi's group, Abbas Bhai stepped forward and drove them himself.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai — a Muslim transport operator — at the wheel of his motor, driving Gandhi toward Dhamtari. A police officer blocking the road, then stepping aside. Abbas Bhai driving on. The ordinary man making the extraordinary journey possible.

slides.text: Days later, the license of Abbas Bhai's transport company Raipur Bus Service was cancelled — punishment for driving Gandhi. He paid with his livelihood for an act of solidarity. The cost of proximity to Gandhi for ordinary people was often everything.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai holding the cancellation notice for his transport license — his face showing loss, but also a quiet pride. His motor sits in the background. The price of conscience. An ordinary man paying an extraordinary cost for a single act of solidarity.

slides.text: On receiving information about Gandhi's arrival, irrigation officials withdrew the anti-farmer order even before the motor reached Dhamtari. The Satyagraha was officially over. But the journey continued — because the movement was larger than one canal.
slides.visualDescription: The withdrawal order arriving in Dhamtari even as Gandhi's motor is still en route. A farmer in Kandel receiving the news. Then: Gandhi's motor approaching Dhamtari through the crowds. The canal issue resolved — the larger struggle just beginning.

slides.text: Makai Chowk, Dhamtari. Within the enclosure of Seth Hussain, a massive crowd gathered. The motor cannot reach the stage through the press of people. At that moment, Omar Seth — a businessman from Gurur — lifted Gandhi on his shoulder.
slides.visualDescription: Makai Chowk, Dhamtari — packed beyond capacity. Gandhi's motor surrounded by humanity. Then: Omar Seth — broad-shouldered, strong — lifting Gandhi onto his shoulders and carrying him through the sea of people toward the stage. Gandhi's hand raised in greeting.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke for an hour at the Dhamtari meeting. He praised Babu Chhotelal Srivastava, Narayan Rao Meghawale, and Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. He made the names of Kandel's heroes known to the 15,000 who had gathered to hear him.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Dhamtari podium, speaking to 15,000 people. The faces of the crowd — rapt, moved, transformed. He is naming the heroes of Kandel. Chhotelal Srivastava in the crowd, hearing his own name spoken by Gandhi. The honour of being seen.

slides.text: Gandhi highlighted non-violence as the foundation of Satyagraha. More than 500 activists from Dhamtari committed to attending the Nagpur session. Bajirao Kridatta presented a bag of Rs 501 to Gandhi — the Tilak Swaraj Fund beginning to fill.
slides.visualDescription: Bajirao Kridatta presenting a bag of Rs 501 to Gandhi at the Dhamtari meeting. Gandhi accepting it with folded hands. 500 activists signing their names for Nagpur. The movement acquiring both momentum and money. The Tilak Fund growing.

slides.text: The massive public meeting in Kankalipara, Raipur — the ground next to Anand Samaj library. A drama had played on this stage the night before. After Gandhi's meeting, those with reverence took bricks from the stage as mementos. The stage was dismantled out of devotion.
slides.visualDescription: Kankalipara ground after Gandhi's meeting — people taking bricks from the stage, reverently, as sacred objects. The stage slowly disappearing piece by piece into the hands of the crowd. Devotion so intense it dismantles what it honours.

slides.text: The women's gathering at Machilabad in Tatyapara — a large number of Muslim women attended openly, donating to the Tilak Fund. Hindu and Muslim women standing together, giving gold and silver, united by a cause larger than any division.
slides.visualDescription: The women's gathering at Machilabad — Muslim and Hindu women standing together, gold rings and bracelets being placed in Gandhi's spread bag. The openness of the donation. Community in action. Unity as the most radical act of the day.

slides.text: Gandhi visited the Jaitasava monastery. That evening, at the meeting near Kankalipara, where now Gandhi Chowk stands, 15,000 people gathered. Gandhi spoke. Shaukat Ali spoke. The Raipur District Congress Committee was born on this night.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi Chowk — the ground where 15,000 stood. Gandhi at the podium with Ali brothers. Ravi Shankar Shukla signing the founding papers of the Raipur DCC by torchlight. Structure emerging from gathering. A permanent organisation born from a single night.

slides.text: Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla was made the first secretary of the Raipur District Congress Committee. From this point, the movement in Chhattisgarh had formal structure — not just inspired individuals, but an organised body capable of sustained action.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla at the table, signing his name as first secretary of the Raipur DCC. Gandhi watching. The formalisation of the movement — paper and ink making permanent what inspiration had started. The organisation that will carry the movement forward.

slides.text: December 22, 1920. Gandhi departs for Nagpur by train. Three days in Chhattisgarh — the Satyagraha supported, a committee formed, thousands mobilised, the Tilak Fund collected. He leaves behind a different Chhattisgarh than the one that received him.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station, December 22, 1920. Gandhi boarding the train to Nagpur. The platform crowd watching him go. Some weeping. Most simply witnessing. The train pulling away slowly. The face at the window: Gandhi's eyes taking in Chhattisgarh one last time.

slides.text: What the Kandel Satyagraha proved: that a false charge could be refused, that organised non-violence could win, that the name of Gandhi was itself a form of power. The canal still flows through Kandel. The paddy still grows. The tax never returned.
slides.visualDescription: Kandel canal today — water flowing, paddy growing, the village at peace. The British order that threatened all of this: withdrawn, forgotten. The victory permanent. A small village that won a Satyagraha against an empire. The canal as testimony.

slides.text: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — the organiser of the Kandel Satyagraha — is the unsung hero at the center of this story. He did not become famous. He did not seek power. He simply refused an unjust tax, organised his community, and won.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — a simple, strong face. The canal behind him. The farmers who followed him around him. He carries no title. He seeks no recognition. He simply did what needed to be done. The most essential kind of hero.

slides.text: Narayan Rao Meghawale, who co-led the Kandel Satyagraha with Srivastava, would later be imprisoned alongside Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. The Satyagraha of Kandel was not a single event — it was the first chapter of a longer commitment.
slides.visualDescription: Narayan Rao Meghawale — standing with Srivastava, Sharma in a post-Satyagraha moment. Three men who did not finish after the canal dispute was settled. Their commitment continuing into prison, into further Satyagrahas, into the rest of their lives.

slides.text: Abbas Bhai lost his transport license. The farmers of Kandel won their water. Ravi Shankar Shukla became the first DCC secretary. Omar Seth carried Gandhi on his shoulders. Each person gave what they had. None of them asked for more than what was right.
slides.visualDescription: A mosaic of the December 1920 visit — Abbas Bhai, the Kandel farmers, Shukla signing documents, Omar Seth lifting Gandhi. Each person in their moment of contribution. The movement made of ordinary people doing extraordinary things.

slides.text: That place is famous today as Gandhi Chowk in Raipur. The ground where 15,000 stood in December 1920 still bears his name. The city grew up around the memory. The chowk as an anchor of historical identity for a city that will not forget.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Gandhi Chowk, Raipur — traffic, modern buildings, the city alive around it. But the name unchanged. Gandhi Chowk. The December 1920 meeting ground, now a busy intersection. The past alive in the name. Memory given an address.

slides.text: The Kandel Canal Satyagraha is the moment when Chhattisgarh joined the national freedom movement as a participant, not merely an observer. Its farmers did not wait for Gandhi to lead them — they led, and then they welcomed him.
slides.visualDescription: The farmers of Kandel in their fields — independent, proud, successful. In the background, Gandhi's train arriving. But the farmers are not looking at the train — they are already working, already free. They won before Gandhi came. He confirmed what they knew.

slides.text: The water of the Kandel canal — refused as taxable theft, reclaimed as a right. The people of Kandel proved that truth, organised and patient, is stronger than an empire. The canal flows today as proof.
slides.visualDescription: Close-up of the Kandel canal water flowing — clear, peaceful, untaxed. The reflection of the sky in the water. The paddy growing on its banks. What was fought for, secured. What was unjust, overturned. The water as testimony to the power of the people.

slides.text: Gandhi is still coming. The Satyagraha is won. But Chhattisgarh wants to see the man. Next: Episode 7 — The Invitation.
slides.visualDescription: A train approaching through the Chhattisgarh landscape at dusk. Its headlight visible through the Sal forest. Inside: Gandhi in a third-class compartment. The land waiting. The people waiting. Title card: Episode 7 — The Invitation.
